utterances.text: Well, in Hrasnica, which was inhabited mostly by Muslims, I felt like a second-class citizen. I experienced this myself when the first barricades were erected, the first barricades around Sarajevo. My friends and neighbours who used to come and help me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Apologies, Your Honour, for the intervention, but evidence like this is of a recurring theme that has to do with suffering of people of Serbian ethnic background and a theme which my colleagues and I have submitted repeatedly is irrelevant to the case at hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not irrelevant in this particular instance. He has referred you to paragraph 7 which says -- this is paragraph 7 of the indictment: "Shortly after Bosnia and Herzegovina was internationally recognised as an independent state on 7th April, armed hostilities broke out in Sarajevo. Even before this date, armed forces supporting the Serbian Democratic Party and elements of the JNA, including units of the 4th Corps, of the 2nd Military District, occupied strategic positions in and around Sarajevo." So that must allow the Defence to lead evidence in relation to the outbreak of hostilities in 1992. So let us see where he is going, you know. But Mr. Tapuskovic knows very well that the Chamber is monitoring very closely the relevance of the evidence that he's leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is there anything I need to explain further, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no, you just need to continue with your examination, bearing in mind the need to ensure that the evidence is relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, once again, as I asked, how did it come about that you became a man who joined the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: After I left Hrasnica after all those events, it all happened spontaneously. We took up weapons to defend our homes, our families. We felt unsafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you live in Trapare --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Trapara, interpreter's correction, where did you live, you Trapara family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we, the Trapara family, have lived in those territories centuries. We are indigenous people. The entire area part of Dobrinja -- parts of Dobrinja, it all belonged to the Trapara family for ages and ages. I came to my family house where my grandmother lived after I left Hrasnica and after all these events I was forced to take up a rifle to defend my family and the land of my grandfather's.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you didn't move anywhere?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: No, I was there all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You were in Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What was happening in Hrasnica? What happened there? Did you have any problems prior to leaving and going to your family house and when was that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: I tried to say that a minute ago, but I was interrupted by the Prosecutor. It was during the time when the first barricades were erected. I came to my house in Kotorac Donji. I had some pigs there and cattle and I went to feed them at my grandmother's. When leaving Hrasnica, my friends and neighbours were at the barricades; they wouldn't let me pass through. And at a certain point a so-called friend put a rifle against my throat and I was forced back. I realised what the situation was, and as soon as I could leave, I went to Donji Kotorac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: As a matter of interest, who is this friend?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said a so-called friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, tell us, why do you say "so-called"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because that man used to work in a bakery where I used to take fodder for my pigs. He knew exactly where my house was and why I was going there, but still he wouldn't let me pass at that moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why? Why wouldn't he let you pass?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably because he knew I was a Serb. I didn't pay much attention to that at the time. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And he was what? What was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A Muslim. The barricades in Hrasnica were put up by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: My last question: What date was it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when the first barricades appeared, but it was in 1992 in any case, March, April, I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we have one moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, and please accept my assurances, I don't do this lightly, but in light of the situation that I indicated earlier on, the objection that I raised earlier on in this witness's testimony with respect to the hill-tops and the elevations, and I could name them if there's a need, a great many of them being on the far side to the north of Sarajevo, far and away outside of the witness's area of responsibility of his brigade and not a single one mentioned in his 65 ter summary. I would like to ask Your Honours' indulgence. I've taken steps while we've been listening to this testimony, working with my colleagues over the e-mail to prepare some maps that I'd like to use in the cross-examination; however, the technology doesn't move that fast, Your Honours, and it takes time to organise people. It takes time to print maps, and with Your Honours' indulgence, I'd like to ask if we could have a pause now rather than later and slightly longer to allow for the maps to be brought to the courtroom, for Mr. Docherty and I to review them, and then I'll certainly be prepared to begin my cross-examination with I think every likelihood of finishing before the end of the day today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What period of time did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps ten minutes longer than the usual break, Your Honour. No more than half an hour. You see that the map just made its way into the courtroom, so the timing is actually perfect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we'll take the break now and resume at a quarter past 12.00, quarter past 12.00. A quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just two matters before the witness comes in. First I neglected to say that in the absence of Judge Mindua, Judge Harhoff and I sit pursuant the provisions of Rule 15 bis. And secondly it's to ask Mr. Tapuskovic whether in relation to the Prosecution's motion mentioned by Mr. Docherty this morning, he would be in a position to respond by Thursday, as requested, bearing in mind that he would be normally entitled to two weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, upon consultation with my colleague, I can inform you that we will be able to submit our response by Thursday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Thanks. Let the witness be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Trapara. My name is Ms. Edgerton, for the Prosecution. I'm going to ask you some questions about your testimony today and I'll try and go as slow as I can, but if for some reason you're unclear or you don't understand the question, please say. Is that all right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you speak a little bit of English or understand a little bit of English, I think. Isn't that correct, Mr. Trapara?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: A bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, just to begin with I wanted to ask you do you understand that a summary of a person's evidence before he testifies here has to be given to the other side, the opposing party. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: A summary of what you are going to talk about usually has to be given by the lawyer for one side to the lawyer for the other side. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And are you aware that the summary of your evidence says that you were in the 2nd Brigade, when you stipulated very definitely that you were a platoon commander in the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you're not in a position to say how that came about then, are you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: I am not. It may have been taken down incorrectly. As of day one, as of the first day of the war, I belonged to the 1st Sarajevo Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And did you tell the Defence you were a soldier or did you tell them you were a platoon commander?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When did you actually join up, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What date was that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: An exact date, yes, the 10th of April, 1994, as stated in the records.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, prior to the 10th of April, 1994, did you have military service?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: Military service, yes, I served my military term in 1987 in Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So what were you doing between April the 6th, 1992, and the time you joined up in the VRS in 1994?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: What was I doing in between?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, what was your function, what was your occupation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: My occupation was an electrician. I worked in the maintenance section at Famos. From 1987 until -- until the beginning of the war, that's where I worked, if I understood your question properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And from 1992 to 1994, what was your function?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: I belonged to the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Uh-huh. So you joined up to the Army of Republika Srpska at the beginning of the war in 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that was in 10th of April, 1992, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And from that point in time you were subordinated to the VRS, you were a part of the VRS, as far as you were concerned?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you were a soldier for an extremely long time, and I would -- I would imagine you're in a position to say how well your unit and your battalion functioned over the course of time. Sounds like it must have been a properly functioning military unit, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Who was your battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: There were several.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of them?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: I do. My battalion commander was the late Bosko Vujadin. Before him, Vuko Coro. Then Bosko Vujadin and then in the end Gavran Dusan, captain.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And who was your brigade commander, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes. The brigade commander was Colonel Veljko Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And was that from the outset of the war up until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: I think Colonel Veljko Stojanovic remained in that position throughout.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not he had a rank in the JNA before the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: I don't. I know he was a colonel in the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Where was your brigade headquarters, do you know?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: My brigade headquarters was in the Lukavica barracks, in -- or rather, at Pavlovci hill.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And how often were you required to make reports which would go up the chain of command to your brigade? Every day? Several times a day?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: I didn't have much to do with the brigade commander. I sent my reports to the company command, who then in turn sent it onwards to the battalion command, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And did you -- how often then would you meet with your company commander or your battalion commander to be briefed or receive instructions?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: There was a meeting daily in the company command, and occasionally there were meetings at the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And -- now, just in terms of your specific function, where were you stationed? What part of the earth did you serve on?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: Most of my time was spent on the line between the Novakovica house and between the old and new airports.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Now, in your testimony you spoke in some measure of detail about elevations around Sarajevo, and you gave the names of a number of different hills, some of which were within your brigade's area of responsibility and some not. Mojmilo, Stupsko Brdo, Zuc, Sokolje, Hum, Grdonj. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So I want to talk then about the elevations a little bit, but first of all, and in line with that, I want you to have a look at the map which appears beside you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And for the record, Your Honours, that map bears the 65 ter number 02617.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Looking at that map, and you can take a little bit of time, would you generally agree that this map shows the elevations around Sarajevo accurately?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: May I approach the map?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Absolutely. Could you say your answer into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, do you see a date on the top left-hand corner of the map?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: Up here?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Left.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: No, that one. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what does the date read?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: The 31st of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, do you see a name on the bottom right-hand corner of the map?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is that the name of Dragomir Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you might not need the map to answer these questions, but you can have it beside you for -- if you need some kind of reference. And I'd like to put this proposition to you. All the hills in your testimony that you mentioned as being controlled by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, isn't it correct that they're actually overlooked by territory in the control of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question. Can you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sure. Now, you listed a number of hills actually ringing Sarajevo on all sides. Now --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- as you said, those were controlled by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, looking at that map, isn't it correct that all of the hills that you mentioned are actually overlooked by territory controlled by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. They don't dominate over each one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see Mr. Tapuskovic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wouldn't want to confuse anyone. There was a half an hour break because of the maps which were provided to us even before that, and this map that is here is not different in any way from the map that is here. There is just a different date on it. And I really don't understand -- well, the witness is being asked something that is not -- not at any point something that he mentioned during his examination-in-chief. What I would like it to be known is that there is no difference between these two maps except in the date and that there was no need for a half an hour break because of that map, because we already had this map which was given to us yesterday. I just don't understand what they want to achieve with this when these two maps are identical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, what I don't understand is the point that you have made. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you said, Mr. Trapara, that they don't dominate over each one, and there may be some exceptions to some of the maps that you mentioned. So perhaps we could go about it this way. Isn't it true that Sarajevo actually sits in a river valley, the valley of the Miljacka river. Sarajevo's in a valley?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: It's not true -- yes, they are in the valley but it's in the valley of the Miljacka river. I said today that there were three rivers that comprise the area of the Sarajevo territory, Miljacka river, Zeljeznica river, and the two of them form the river Bosna. So it's well-known through which areas of the town the Miljacka flows, the Zeljeznica flows, and through which parts of the town the Bosna River flows. All this is known.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But Sarajevo's in a valley?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. And isn't it --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: In a depression.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Isn't it true that hills like Zuc and Hum are actually high points in the valley?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But all of these points, isn't it true, were overlooked by higher elevations controlled by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps? And have a look at that map if you need some assistance.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: It's not necessary. They were below higher elevations, but these were dominant points over the population of Sarajevo. You couldn't fire at the town from Jahorina or Hresa or from other hills. I've forgotten the exact names. The hills that I've cited were dominant and they were used for fire by the Muslim army against the Serb army and the civilian population of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you're a platoon commander, sir, so as a platoon commander you're probably -- and you were in the army for four years, so you're probably aware of how mortars are used. Is that right? You've seen them in action?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, I do know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And so then you must be aware that mortar crews can hit a target that they can't see?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that's why they call mortars indirect fire weapons?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What kind of heavy weapons are in -- were in possession of your brigade from August 1994 to November 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: All the artillery weapons were removed from 15 to 35 kilometres, I'm not sure about the distance, but they were out of range of the Sarajevo area. There was an order that all the heavy artillery had to be removed from their positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, can I ask you to turn to the map behind you then and look in the area of responsibility of your brigade because it's set out on the map and ask you to find Tvrdemici on the map. And you'll see some lettering in Cyrillic in black letters ...

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: I cannot find it. I don't see where it is written here, but I know exactly where that location is.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the name.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My mispronunciation of the name, Madam interpreter, it's Tvrdemici, if that gives you some hint.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If you can find in the area of response --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I know, Tvrdemici, Tvrdemici, it's a location above Sarajevo. It's some 15 kilometres away from my house in the direction of Jahorina, but I cannot find that here. I know exactly where it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can you look at that map, sir, and in the area of responsibility of your brigade find the black lettering that reads in Cyrillic "KAG 2." You found it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The notations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I cannot see what is being shown here. I agree, we can use that map to point out things, but I don't understand why we're not using this other map that is much more enlarged and it's easier to spot things on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why aren't you using the bigger map, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic's map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is that the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, the bigger one. I don't want to personalise it. It's the bigger map.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, the Prosecution's entitled to choose whatever exhibits they might have -- they might wish to put as part of their cross-examination. And if it would assist, in e-court 02617E or 03326 are cut-outs of the area that the witness is pointing to so that everybody is able to see clearly what he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Tapuskovic, you have your answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So now you found Tvrdemici. Now, the notations that you found, would you agree with me, those notations KAG 2 and the numbers below them represent the brigade artillery battery, don't they? 155 -- pardon me?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: I didn't really know the abbreviations, so I really cannot agree with you. I don't know what KAG means.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you wouldn't agree with me then that the notations there 155/4 represent an artillery battery of 455-millimetre howitzers?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: I've already told you, I can't see what's written there, but I really don't know what the abbreviation stands for, if it's a howitzer or something else. It could be something else. I really don't know what that means.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps then I could ask you to turn to your screen and ask that 65 ter number 03326 be brought up. That's a cut-out of the area beside you on the map. You should be able to see more clearly now. I also see T-130. T denotes a tank, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: Well, I keep telling you but it seems to be in vain. I don't know what the indications are. I don't know what H-130 means, what the other abbreviations stand for, what the VLR-128 means. I mean, it could be a tank or -- I don't know, but it's something that I really cannot talk about because I don't know what it stands for.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So are you saying that you, despite giving evidence in detail about elevations and who controlled the elevations, that you are not able to discuss the notations on a military map?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: I cannot talk about abbreviations and the markings, but I can talk about the places that are shown on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And are you -- would you disagree with me, Mr. Trapara, if I put to you that the abbreviation KAR is an acronym for the Corps Artillery Group?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: I can agree with you that it means that, but it can mean something else as well. KAG can mean a thousand different things. I can translate or interpret abbreviations in the Serbian language in a hundred different ways. I don't know. Maybe that's what it stands for, but I don't know that. I was never in the corps command. I cannot know what they wrote down and what that meant. I wasn't an active-duty military personnel and I was just a regular civilian.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the rest of his answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Witness, the interpreter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, Witness, could you repeat the rest of your answer. The last thing we have is: " ... I was just a regular civilian." What did you say after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I was just a regular soldier and a platoon commander of the army of Republika Srpska, so I don't know what the higher command responsibilities would involve and I don't know what that particular thing could mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But you're not disagreeing with me, are you, that this could designate a Corps Artillery Group within the area of responsibility of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: I do not agree with you. It could be an abbreviation, but again I keep saying that I don't know what that means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that my colleague now is placing herself in the role of the witness. The witness should not -- should be asked to say what he could know, but now he is being asked to do something and it's as if my colleague was herself testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There's nothing abnormal about that kind of questioning, and the witness has answered it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: A couple more questions about this map, Mr. Trapara. If we can go a little bit further up to the north, still in the area of responsibility of your brigade, immediately above the letters which designate your brigade's name, for Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade, you see notation with the abbreviation in Cyrillic BRAG-1. Would you agree with me that that notation represents the Brigade Artillery Group and its position?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know the abbreviations. I cannot agree with you because I don't know the abbreviations. I cannot claim to know something that I don't know. In Serbian there are many abbreviations, BR can mean number; AG can mean aggregate, generator, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So I take your answer saying you don't recognise the abbreviations, but are you disagreeing with the accuracy of weapons placements as depicted on this map signed by Dragomir Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: I don't know if they had been placed there. How could I know as a soldier who was on the front line where our artillery had gone? I don't know how far this is from Sarajevo. There are maybe some 15 to 20 kilometres from my house to the Tvrdimici.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, sir, you testified about locations further than 15 to 20 kilometres away from your house when you talked about elevations held by the Bosnian -- the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So I naturally assumed that you would know of the situation in terms of weapons within your brigade's actual area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: I'm not saying that there weren't any. There were weapons and positions, but I don't know where the weapons were. I was talking about the hills above Sarajevo. Tvrdimici is not a hill above Sarajevo. It's I don't know how many kilometres away from Sarajevo. I was talking about fire from rifles or automatic rifles or machine-guns from the hills overlooking the area. I didn't talk about this at any point.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you then, Mr. Trapara.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I wonder if I could ask this map, Your Honour, and the cut-out, so that would be 02617 for the map and the cut-out at 03362 [sic] admitted as exhibits, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 02617 will be admitted as P788; and 65 ter number 03326 will be admitted as P789.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Trapara, what do you know about the use of air-bombs by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps against Bosnian-held territory?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: Air-bombs?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: I don't know about air-bombs. There were no planes. As far as I know the Army of the Republika Srpska didn't have any planes, they weren't able to use planes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So are you saying you don't have any information about extremely high-calibre 250-kilogramme bombs launched from mobile modified launchers against Bosnian-held territory in 1994 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: I don't know about that -- just one moment. How could I have any knowledge about that then because it would turn out that the Army of Republika Srpska had planes. So the question is not clear to me. As far as I know, the Army of Republika Srpska didn't have planes and it wasn't able to use air-bombs.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What I was actually asking about, sir, was extremely powerful bombs, originally air-bombs, modified so that they could be launched from mobile ground launchers. In fact, one impacted on a location in Hrasnica very close to you in April 1995. Are you aware of that incident?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: No, no, I cannot understand that such an air-bomb could have been dropped an Hrasnica. It's something that I'm hearing for the first time. You're talking about a launcher -- well, I don't know. Hrasnica was dominant. Igman was above, and Igman is the highest mountain from which the entire of Sarajevo was controlled. So I don't know about this. This is the first time that I'm hearing of this from you. Perhaps the best thing would be for you to explain what you consider an air-bomb to be. I cannot understand that that exists. As far as I know, an air-bomb is launched from an aeroplane. Well, as for anything else, this is the first time I'm hearing about that from you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can I ask P225 be brought up on the screen for Mr. Trapara, please. And I think the B/C/S version -- both versions will have to go to page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir, this is a daily combat report from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps to the VRS Main Staff signed by Dragomir Milosevic. Now, at page 2, paragraph 2 -- now I see two English versions on the screen. Yeah. Page 2, paragraph 2, under the heading "our forces," you see an entry that says: "In Ilidza a 250-kilo air-bomb was launched at the centre of Hrasnica ..." Do you see the line I'm referring to? It's at the very top of your page in your language, second line.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: I see that. What it says, "In the Ilidza pbr one 120-millimetre mine was fired and one 250-kilogramme aerial air-bomb was launched at the centre of Hrasnica. According to the interception centre the Muslims claim that the 'Luna' rocket had dropped or was dropped."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, are you saying that this is news to you, that the SRK launched an aerial bomb at Hrasnica in 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: What it says here is the Ilidza Brigade, and this is on the other side completely, and this is the first time that I'm hearing about that. It's completely on the other side of Ilidza. I don't know -- I didn't know that there was an air-bomb that could have been dropped from somewhere other than an aeroplane. As far as I'm concerned, that is a completely new thing for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So then, sir, you wouldn't know anything about the storage of pieces or components of air-bombs in the Kotorac barracks in May 1995 then, would you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: In Kotorac barracks?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: Kotorac never had a barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have document bearing the ter number 03214 up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So this, sir, is a document dated 12 May 1995 from Lieutenant-Colonel Solar to the VRS Main Staff logistics, stating that on personal inspection of the brigade he found four pieces of 250-kilo air-bombs, saying the brigade failed to inform them about them. Does this change your mind about weapons being stored in Kotorac?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: It says here: "While touring the 2nd Slpbr in the Kotorac barracks. " This is the 2nd Brigade, it's not the area of responsibility of my brigade, Srbl.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, sir, Gornji Kotorac and Donji Kotorac being so proximate to one another I would have thought you would have known something about what went on in that location when you were so quick to speak about who controlled hills around Sarajevo far and away outside of the area of responsibility of your corps. Are you saying you don't know anything about what was in the Kotorac barracks?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: A barracks didn't exist in Kotorac. Gornji Kotorac or upper Kotorac is the place of Vojkovici, actually I understand that now. That's where the barracks was Vojkovici. Kotorac, Gornji, Donji, does not have a barracks. Probably there was a mistake. There was a military warehouse there, but I never had access there. But maybe this is a mistake in the name here.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. Kotorac was populated. What they mean probably is Vojkovici. That could be the mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With that answer, Your Honour, I'd ask that this document be admitted as the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P790, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: One last question in relation to air-bombs, sir, what do you know about plans to use these air-bombs that we've been talking about on Donji Kotorac?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps if I had a document pulled up on the screen in front of you, you would be able to understand just a bit more clearly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Ter number is 02324, it's P703.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You see it now. It's a 26 April 1995 report from the SRK command, head of artillery, Tadija Manojlovic, to the General Staff confirming that on that date a decision was reached to drop air-bombs on the entrance to the tunnel at Donji Kotorac and Hrasnica. Looking at that document, Mr. Trapara, does that refresh any recollection you might have about the use of air-bombs in your immediate vicinity, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: Well, it says here it's the area of responsibility of the Igman Brigade, that's not my brigade. I really don't know about this. If such an air-bomb existed, it could have been fired from Ilidza, if it existed. I don't know that it did, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir, have you ever met the accused in this case personally?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the precise date. I think when he was appointed corps commander, Mr. Dragomir Milosevic, he went to inspect the entire unit and then he came to inspect my platoon also.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So he came to the trenches where you were serving, you and your unit?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Was that on one occasion -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: He didn't actually enter the trench, but he came to the front line.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Was that on one occasion or more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: I think it was on two occasions. I'm not absolutely sure. I know it was at least once. I'm not sure about the second time, but it was once or twice as far as Kotorac Donji is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And so the only time you met him is when he came to your post, in fact?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But you've said before that you weren't a member of the senior corps staff, so then I take from that that you wouldn't have participated in any decision-making at the corps level. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So even at the time of the general's visit to your post, you weren't involved of or aware of orders that might have been issued regarding the shelling of Bosnian-held territory, the sniping, or the use of these air-bombs that we've been talking about, would you have?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: Can you repeat your last question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Not being a member of the senior corps staff, you weren't involved or aware of any orders that might have been issued within that corps group or even discussed within that corps group regarding the shelling of Bosnian-held territory, the sniping, or the use of air-bombs, would you have?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: I can't know that. I know there was an express order at my line of responsibility. There was never a sniper, and our orders were not to shoot during the cease-fire from any kind of weapon. Well, I don't know what happened elsewhere, but I know about my platoon. I know what orders we received from the high-ranking command.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's fine, and I certainly accept that. But now because of the situation, of course, during the period of the indictment, in fact probably from very early on in the war in 1992, you never went into Bosnian-held territory, did you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: From 1992 onwards, I never went on to the territory controlled by the BH government. I was always on the territory of Republika Srpska. Had I gone there, I would never have come back.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Obviously it was, at a certain level, dangerous for any number of reasons, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: There was great hatred.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But wouldn't you agree that there was also great risk of being hit by rifle-fire, gun-fire, mortar fire? The people who were inside the confrontation lines - and that included Serb civilians - were at great risk every day for their lives. Wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: Serb civilians? I don't understand your question. I don't understand what you're getting at. That it was very risky to go on to the territory held by the Bosnian Muslims. Is that what you're asking? That's how I understood your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You said that it was risky because there was great hatred, but that wouldn't have been the only risk if you would have made your way or found yourself inside the confrontation lines, would it have? You could have been shot any day. You could have been injured or killed by mortar fire any day, couldn't you have? So the --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My house, where I lived, where I slept, was 2 or 300 metres away from the front line, and it was exposed to sniper fire and barrage fire on a daily basis and shelling as well from the Muslim side. And after a certain period of time when my late mother was killed, they even killed my dog.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I -- sir, you know we extend our sympathies for what you went through in your location and in your situation. But as one Prosecution witness said earlier in this case, there was no monopoly on suffering; both sides suffered. Wasn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: Well, that's a fact. It was wartime.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And my question to you, sir, was really focused on picking up what you had said in your testimony about the risks of being inside the confrontation lines. While there may well have been strong feelings or, as you said, great hatred, there was also great risk from shelling and sniping or, in fact, some winters from freezing or going hungry, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: No. As for fire, yes, there was shooting from both sides. But as for going hungry, I don't know how they lived there, what they ate, whether they had food, I can't know. There are various kinds of beverages, but many people became rich after the war. All that's Muslim propaganda. I don't believe it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't have any further questions, Mr. Trapara. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Any re-examination, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have some questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now that we're dealing with the issue raised by my learned friend about going hungry and about food, what was the situation like on your side as regards food?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: Well, after the sanctions imposed by Serbia on Republika Srpska, our situation was worse than theirs. They were being financed by the whole world. They brought food to Sarajevo by plane. 90 per cent of the food that came to Sarajevo was sent to the town. Nothing reached the Serb parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that your first commander, because you answered a question about who your commanders were, you said the first was the late Bosko Vujadin. How did he become late?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: He was killed in 1992 or 1993 in an ambush, he and another soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: After that my learned friend asked you something about indirect shooting, and I'm asking you now whether one can shoot indirectly if one does not see the target?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: No, one can't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You were shown this map to your right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Wasn't indirect shooting, firing, a reference to mortars? Ms. Edgerton, the -- you had asked some questions about --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- indirect firing.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. At page 58 my question was: "You must be aware that mortar crews can hit a target that they can't see?" And the answer was: "Yes, of course." And then I asked whether -- if that was why -- that's why they called mortars indirect fire weapons, and the witness then agreed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that what you're referring to, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Then you haven't represented it accurately. The cross-examination related to indirect firing from mortars, and the witness did agree that that was possible. And we have heard evidence in this case about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He said that it was possible, but let him then explain about this. Indirect firing is possible, but is indirect firing possible -- well, let him explain what he understands by "indirect firing" and whether it's possible to fire indirectly if one does not see the target one is aiming at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask him because we have had enough evidence on that in the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's one thing to fire at random and quite another thing to fire indirectly because any targeting, whether it's indirect or not, is at a target. Random firing is something quite different. So I'm asking whether it's possible to fire indirectly from a mortar without seeing the target one is aiming at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, you want to put that question to the witness? Because you didn't put that question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the question I want to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. That's the question you should have put originally. Witness, what is the answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I first understood Mr. Tapuskovic to be referring to shooting from a rifle. That's why I said it was impossible to do it indirectly. With mortars, it's very difficult to fire indirectly. You have to see your target. That's my opinion, but I don't really know a lot about mortars. There was not a single mortar at the line that I was at. It was all only infantry weapons where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I approach the map for ten seconds, just to take a look at it so I can put a question about it. Can I approach the large map and take a look at it so I can put my question to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If you can take a look at the exact date on that map.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: The 31st of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you know what the witness who drew up this map said about when it was made, but that's a matter of comparison and it's not for this witness. I would like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My friend may be mistaken, but this map wasn't yet in evidence, so I don't understand first of all his comment what the witness who drew-up this map said about it when it was made, and I would object to his comment as being inappropriate as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Refrain from comments of that kind. Refrain from all comments. Ask questions that relate to the evidence, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I may be wrong, but I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But only the 31st of August, 1995, do you remember what stage the conflict was in on that date, what was happening around that time at the separation lines. Do you remember what happened then on the 31st of August, 1995 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Don't answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, but with respect, that's not something that arises from the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How does it arise, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my learned friend showed the witness a map dated the 31st of August, 1995. We dealt with these maps. The 31st of August, 1995, was the first day of the NATO air-strikes. That's why it's important. Does the witness know what went on in those days, around that time, because this is a map from the end of the war and it was formed under the most difficult wartime circumstances. That's why the date of the map is so important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but are you proposing now to elicit evidence about the NATO air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, but I want to ask whether the witness knows what was happening around the 31st of August, 1995, because this is directly linked to the characteristics of this map. The positions that have been entered in here correspond to that point in time. That's not the point in time when heavy weapons were excluded. That was in February, and the weapons were returned later on. This was the time of the greatest offensive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Move on, Mr. Tapuskovic. We rule that it doesn't arise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Well, let's look at P789, that's a Prosecution exhibit, it's another map.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you indicate on this map the place where Donji Kotorac is located and can you mark it, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I actually even had to check with my colleague, but how does this arise from cross, asking one to mark a new location on a map that's been entered into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Don't mark anything. Mr. Tapuskovic, what is this about?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we listened to what my learned friend dealt with about the positions of these weapons that the witness said he knew nothing about, when he shows where Kotorac is, then it will follow quite logically that from the place where he was, there were no heavy weapons nearby marked in any way. You can see that Donji Kotorac is on the separation line itself, and looking at this map within 8 kilometres of that location, if each of these squares represents 2 kilometres, there were no heavy weapons anywhere close. So when he shows where Donji Kotorac is, this will become quite clear in relation to the positions my learned friend was insisting on, Donji Kotorac, if he only shows where it is and marks it, and nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm reinforced in my objection, Your Honour, now that I've heard my friend's submission. This is squarely not something that he's entitled to do in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is not the purpose of re-examination. Move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at P225, P225 -- or rather, P790. I didn't note it down correctly. It was those documents. Just a moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was right the first time, 790.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you must get a move on. Let us move on. Either you have a question or you don't. If you don't, we'll conclude.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was right the first time. I said P790.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This document was shown to you my learned friend, and she insisted on the barracks. Please read the first paragraph where reference is made to these matters while visiting. What does it say here, please?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: "While visiting the 2nd Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade in the Kotorac barracks we discovered by personal inspection that they possessed four pieces of 250-kilogramme M-72 aerial bombs without fuses and rocket tensions and with mechanically damaged stabilisers and bomb bodies. We did not know that the bombs existed and the brigade failed to inform us about them."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you and the next sentence.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: "According to their information, FAB were recently dug out in the Krupac stone pit during engineering works. We ask you to --"

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you draw any conclusion from this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN TRAPARA
utterances.text: I've already said I never heard of this. I didn't know it existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But that's food for thought and that's not your job. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for giving it. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Next witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we were informed that the witness is experiencing some ear pain, so he's not readily available here at the Tribunal; otherwise he is here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, is this the witness? I see. Okay. Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And you may begin, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, tell us your last and first name, please.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC
utterances.text: My name is Stjepan Djukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You were born on the 15th of January, 1972?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please wait for the entire question to be recorded before answering. So far this has been working because the questions and answers were short, but please wait for my question to be recorded completely. You were born in Hadzici, in Ilijas municipality?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You completed your primary education in Ilijas?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You completed your secondary education in Ilidza in 1992?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What were you supposed to do right after you completed your education?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC
utterances.text: After I completed my education I was supposed to serve under the laws of the then-FRY, and having turned 18 I was supposed to serve my military term.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you begin with your military service?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC
utterances.text: I began my military service on the 15th of March, 1991, in Banja Luka. I was to be trained as a member of the armoured mechanised unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This was March 1991 when you went to serve your military term. What did you feel like?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC
utterances.text: To be honest, at that time anyone coming from -- or being of Serbian ethnic background considered serving a military term an honour; therefore, I went to do that gladly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were you able to foresee that anything unpleasant or problematic might await you while you served your military term?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC
utterances.text: At the time when I left, when I was getting ready to join the JNA, at that time I wasn't even contemplating any unpleasant situations or problems that I might encounter there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please explain to us the following. You were in Banja Luka. Were there any changes and when did problems begin occurring?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC
utterances.text: Upon my arrival in the JNA, in Banja Luka, to the training centre for armoured and mechanised units in Zaluzani, there were no problems, there were no unpleasant situations and I couldn't foresee any of that coming any time soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As a soldier, what were you supposed to do? Were you trained in anything?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC
utterances.text: Upon my arrival into the barracks at Zaluzani to the training centre for armoured and mechanised units, I was trained to be a driver of the T-55 tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Concerning the rest of your service with the JNA, were you transferred anywhere and what was going on?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to allow more time for me to be able to explain my military term with the JNA in full with your following questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Please let us explain whether you were transferred and what was happening. Did you become upset over anything at a certain point in time?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC
utterances.text: I understand your question. After the initial training period was completed in Banja Luka, I was transferred to Bjelovar in the Republic of Croatia. Upon my arrival in Bjelovar, I was quite surprised by the unusual situation I encountered. There was a great concern in the barracks, since the barracks were without electricity, water, and within its perimeter there were embankments for the soldiers who were supposed to stand guard. In the dorm --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. I understand your need to discuss such details, but tell me some of the key things since we need to move along faster.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. I stayed there for some five to seven days. In the town we could hear firing, and I prayed God that I leave Belgrade and be transferred -- Bjelovar and be transferred somewhere else. And thankfully, that happened. I left Bjelovar for Koprivnica. As opposed to Bjelovar, things were quite calmer there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When did you encounter problems?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC
utterances.text: After a short while, the problems began in Slunj. We were in the field. We were supposed to establish a buffer zone there between Serbs and Croats, so as try and prevent conflicts. After that we were transferred to Varazdin, where problems escalated. In the second half of June, I believe, or towards end June, there were great problems in Slovenia. For us, the young soldiers there, it had a great negative impact and the pervading atmosphere encompassed the entire barracks in Varazdin. We were provoked from outside the perimeter of the barracks. People were trying to persuade us that we should desert, that we should skip the army since we had nothing to do with that. We were put under psychological pressure, and speakers were mounted around the barracks --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me exactly what happened, something that was more important. When was the situation the worst? Please move along more speedily.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC
utterances.text: I have to state that what followed was basically a siege of the barracks. There was no electricity. We had to pump water and until the 18th of October the situation remained as such. It was then that fire was opened on the barracks, a soldier was wounded, and I think we also had several soldiers killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, it's about time for the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Maybe this would help to change the character of things for our recommencement tomorrow morning, Your Honour, but I rise on the point of relevancy, in the first place, because we're still outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina; and secondly, this is completely outside of what was disclosed as what might be this witness's potential testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I've been giving the witness a little time to come to something that is more pertinent, and tomorrow we will see whether he has anything to offer that is relevant. Please bear that in mind, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 27th day of June, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.
